utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record everyone is present, including the accused, except Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Haynes, and Mr. Bourgon. Good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to welcome you again, once more. Mr. Vanderpuye, could you conclude, please, your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. And good afternoon to my colleagues. And good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, yesterday when we were -- before we concluded we spoke about your expertise in assessing the functional responsibility of various Main Staff members. In particular in respect of the decision-making process regarding UNPROFOR and international humanitarian convoys, do you have any specific expertise in terms of evaluating the functional responsibility of the individuals that were involved in that process?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this expert report, I provided just a summary. And since -- in studying all the materials available to me, I saw that in the process of proposing and making decisions, General Miletic's name did not exist, I made the summary very short. I started with that option, but I gave up on it, and it did not finally enter my final expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it, then, that you don't have any familiarity with the role that was played by Slavko Kralj in the process involved of convoy approvals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the process because I did not analyse that organisational unit separately. I knew of its existence. I knew what it was intended for, what its purpose was, and who it was tied to. And when I looked at all the aspects of the organisation, I saw that it went beyond the topic of my research, and I decided not to dwell upon and go into any greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So just for the record the same would be true, therefore, for Radoslav Pandzic, Milos Djurdjic, Milan Gvero, Zdravko Tolimir; that's true, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He needs to ask individually about those people, particularly the accused, quite obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I know, perhaps, it was your intention to rise and make the submission, but he has already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, but I accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not recorded though, but he said yes. Do you confirm, General, that you answered "yes" to Mr. Vanderpuye's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm that I said "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Terms of General Miletic's role as chief of the Administration for Operations and Training, you did evaluate that pursuant to the rules and pursuant to his position in the establishment; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid does not fall under the systemic organisation of the organisation and functioning of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I evaluated the position of the Administration for Operations and Training, and General Miletic's position based on all the relevant documents that were important and that regulated the functioning of humanitarian aid. And based on my evaluation on that algorithm, I arrived at a conclusion that I incorporated into my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you recognise and you can confirm that the position that was occupied by General Miletic in 1995 as chief of the administration of training -- operations and training was a significant and important one within the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to confirm your sentence, I have to be a bit more precise than yourself. The position that was performed by General Miletic as the chief of the Administration for Operations and Training is a very important organisational unit in the staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your report, you refer to the term "standing in," and you define that for us as necessitating a written order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please direct me to where I mention this word "acting on behalf of --" as far as I can remember, I used the word "standing in for" and "replacing" or "deputising."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have a problem in terms of the translation, and that's all. What I said was and my question was that you did talk about the term "standing in" in your report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in defining that during your testimony you indicated that it required a written order; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was very precise, and I said that "standing in for" is a situation in the service which is regulated by the law, and if for this situation to be functioning properly it requires an appropriate order, and only then can it function. Without an order of that kind, this "standing in" situation cannot exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the rules that you indicated that provide a commander with a certain amount of flexibility in the implementation of its modality, would that account for a situation where a person might stand in without a written order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Standing in for as a situation in service was not flexible and did not allow much room for flexibility. In order for somebody to stand in for somebody else, they had to meet certain criteria that such a position required. Standing in for without an order to stand in for would certainly not function because a large number of organisational units that are tied to that organisational unit would not be duty-bound to accept or carry out any order or any material document, anything that arises from the rights and duties of that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the process of reviewing the material that you used for your -- your report, you did, obviously, review numerous documents where General Miletic signed as standing in for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed many documents bearing different signatures, and I also reviewed documents that were signed by General Miletic who was replacing the Chief of Staff; whereas, the document depicted the word "stand in for," and then I established the relationship with -- between how it was signed and the factual situation. And based on that, I created certain relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you referred to the fact that General Miletic signed in the capacity of standing in for the Chief of Staff during your testimony as a rather unfortunate way of signing his name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be a translation problem, but I will be precise. I never said that General Miletic signed any document standing in for the Chief of Staff. Actually, the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska, because he never stood in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about two different things. One, you are talking about the factual question of whether he stood in for him; in the other sense we are talking about whether or not his name appears on any document as standing in. What I am referring to is the latter. You did, in fact, review documents where General Miletic's name appears as standing in for the Chief of Staff; that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you testified that it was an unfortunate way of signing his name, and that's what you were referring to, the fact that it appears on those documents in that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this typed block signature, and I assumed if the document was dispatched in this way with that block signature that the document itself was signed, and if it, indeed, was -- and I never saw any document with original signature. If it was signed then it is true what I stated that this was a misfortunate situation and a way for him to devise the best possible solution under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In fact, you said that the reason why he signed that way was because of a situation concerning the way General Milovanovic preferred that he signed such documents; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that this kind of signing documents in such an awkward way is the consequence of the best solution devised by the two of them, and I also bore in mind the strict -- the official statement by General Manojlo who signed on behalf of General Miletic, and where it was stated that he was a very consistent officer which means that he never encroached his authorities, that he never violated any of his authorities, that he never signed anything that he was not entitled to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if we could, could I have, please, 65 ter 5D00753 in e-court, please. 723, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have in front of you is a personnel assessment regarding General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could go to page -- it should be 3 in the English, and it may be the second page in the B/C/S. Okay, well, we have the B/C/S in front. I think there has been a mistake in terms of loading the document. I can read the English into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have before you, General, is a descriptive assessment and conclusion regarding General Miletic's performance. The period covers 1990 to 1994. And it's a document that is signed by Manojlo Milovanovic. It is also signed by General Miletic. And is dated 12th May, 1995. It reads as follows in the second paragraph: "His relationship with colleagues, subordinates, and superiors, is fair, moderate, and shows due respect --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to see the next page in English, please. There is no page English, only the first page? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye. And sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It reads in the second paragraph: "His relationship with colleagues, subordinates, and superiors, is fair, moderate, and shows due respect. Through his actions and personal example he is a strong cohesive factor to where he lives and works, and much credit goes to him for the unity and success of activities of the Main Staff of the VRS and immediate subordinate command." Immediately preceding it says at the bottom of the first paragraph that: "He especially stands out in the field of general analytics and operations and strategy, and he makes all his draft decisions and decisions on the basis of real facts without displaying emotions, partiality, glossing over, and the like." In the conclusion it reads that: "He is a highly educated, competent, conscientious officer of high moral qualities, who greatly contributes to the success of the VRS in the battle-field through his diligent performance of his duty." And he's given a grade of excellent. General Miletic clearly knows the difference between standing in and not standing in. That's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of things that are relevant for this section that you have read out to me. First of all, the translator, the interpreter said that this was the personnel assessment. In fact, it is the official assessment. And later on, the interpreter said that this was a quality assessment. In fact, it is a personnel assessment that is based as a -- it is used as a basis for promotion or transfer. And you told me that General Miletic, apparently, is aware of the difference between "replacing" and "standing in for." The only segment in this assessment is the one that is on the previous page that was written by General Miletic himself. All the rest was actually written by General Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Certainly you're not suggesting that General Miletic doesn't know the difference between "standing in" and "not standing in." I take it that's not what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. I think that he knows the difference between "standing in" and "replacing."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 4160, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document that you have in front of you is from the Army of Yugoslavia and General Staff. Its indicated -- its dated 21 February 2000 and indicates a title of minutes composed at the army of Yugoslavia General Staff on 31 January 2000 regarding the official interview conducted with Major General Radivoje, son of Mitar Miletic, in relation to the ending of his professional military service. In the English if we could go to the second page. I think if we can go down a page in the B/C/S, I want to direct your attention to what I am referring to. In the B/C/S version it is the next-to-last paragraph, although there is not a space between them. And in the English it's the second paragraph. From the top of the page, it reads as follows: "During the war I was on duty of the chief of operations and training administration in the Army of Yugoslavia General Staff 30th Personnel Centre, and for a certain period I was representing the deputy chief of VRS Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff. I am used to work. It is hard for me to receive salary and not to work." Now, in respect of this particular paragraph, there is written in the English "representing the deputy chief of the VRS." Do you read that in the version that is written in your language?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Does that have a specific military meaning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case it does have a very specific military meaning. I don't know how General Nikolic missed that. He's a great expert for human resources for personnel, and I don't know how that was skipped by General Miletic himself. Because now we have a post that never existed in the Main Staff of the VRS that is now mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And in the transcript we have a reference at page 10, line 11, where you refer to General Nikolic. Is that accurate, is that what you meant to say, or is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the conversation was held by General Stamenko Nikolic as -- in his official capacity, he was highly regarded as an expert for personnel issues in the army, and General Miletic was also present there. And I said that I found it strange that it skipped past him, that they missed the fact that the mention is made here of a post that never existed in the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, what should the post be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is what post or what duty, because we could not really see that. You could actually opt for anything. Let me tell you what this duty should be precisely and how it should be described precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If General Miletic mentioned that he stood in for anybody, who would that be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the rules, General Miletic could be designated to stand in for any person who occupies a post with the same requirements that he possesses, that he meets, and if you are hinting that he should be standing in for the Chief of the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska, which I don't think that he said, then the formulation, the wording would be as follows. That would be the post. In a certain period of time, I stood in for the Chief of Staff of the staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. So this would be a precisely defined duty, and this is what I said on my first day here, how this duty or this post is defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In all of the documents that you reviewed in preparation for your testimony and in preparation -- and in preparing your report, it's fair to say that you didn't see General Miletic's name attached to any document as standing in for anybody or any post other than Chief of Staff of the staff of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer the question, please, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we ask the witness to please take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, could you remove your headphones, please. Yes, we can proceed, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document that we have before us is in regard to all of the service of General Miletic within the Army of the Republika Srpska. I am not saying that it was possible or not possible, but we don't know. At some time, at some point in time, he did represent the head of the Administration for Operations and Training. It was possible that he did so in 1992 and 1993. And surely, the witness never had an opportunity to look at documents pertaining to 1992 and 1993. Nothing in this document indicates that this period is 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Ms. Fauveau. I think that deserves feedback from you, some remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My understanding is that it was this witness's objective to determine the capacity in which General Miletic signed certain documents as standing in for the Chief of Staff. That is the thrust of his expert report. This is a document that is clearly relevant to that subject matter in so far as it concerns General Miletic's service during the period of time in question. It is his retirement exit statement, as it were. And what he talks about is -- he says very specifically that "During the war --" he talks about his service during the war. This is a relevant and obviously salient issue with respect of determining what his capacity was during the war which is what the subject matter of his expert opinion and his testimony is about. I think it's a reasonable question to put to the witness, particularly since the witness has expertise in organisational structure of the VRS, particularly the Main Staff, particularly the positions that General Miletic has alleged in the indictment and in the documents to occupy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, before I consult with my colleagues, I think that your answer, your remark, your response, is not exactly responsive to the point made by Ms. Fauveau. I think what Ms. Fauveau pointed out was the following, essentially: If you look at this particular paragraph, what is being stated there spans over the entire period of the war. What she is objecting to is you presenting this paragraph to the witness in conjunction or related to the documents where he signed as standing in for the Chief of Staff. In other words, what she is suggesting is that you should be fairer with the witness and put to him also that this paragraph doesn't necessarily refer to 1995 but to the entire period of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my question - and I don't have it in front of me - was whether or not in all of the documents that he had reviewed, whether he had ever come across General Miletic standing in for anybody other than the Chief of Staff, because the question related to whether or not this -- he specifically mentioned that this post that is identified on this document doesn't exist. Never existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what Madam Fauveau is tell you is that it could have been in 1992 or 1993 or 1994 that he could have stood in or represented someone else rather than the Chief of Staff and that someone else is being described erroneously according to the witness as deputy chief of the Army of Republika Srpska. This is what she is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's a fair suggestion, but I don't think that that relates to the characterization of the document. That is something that the expert can clearly distinguish. If he's saying that that post never existed in the Army of Republika Srpska ever during the war, then clearly there is an error on this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, then ask him what he understands when he reads this document. Who - and you have already actually asked him - who could have General Miletic represented or meant to say he represented in this paragraph? And leave it at that. Let me consult with my colleagues in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, prevailing opinion here in addition is that we proceed with the witness answering the question, and you can deal with this matter yourself on further redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, in respect of this document I had asked you whether you had seen in the -- in all the documents that you reviewed, preparing to testify and preparing your report, whether you had ever seen General Miletic's signature as standing in for anyone besides the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite clear a little while ago that I never saw any documents about standing in that were signed by him. I merely saw the signature block. And since this document was disseminated, then I think that he did stipulate that, but I think that I did see a document where he is indicated as "standing in" for somebody, but he was never in Bosnia and Herzegovina at all at that time. I can't now tell you what report this is, give you the precise reference, but I think that it exists somewhere, but I did not see any other documents indicating that he was "standing in for."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, since you prepared your report, you've had an opportunity to actually review a collection of documents that we have concerning General Miletic. Let me just share with you a couple of the things that we found. I will say that the collection of documents that we have are by no means complete, but in the collection that we found, in reviewing 587 documents attributed to General Miletic, 579 of those documents were attributed to him as standing in for the Chief of Staff. Those documents consisted of combat reports, they consisted of documents relating to humanitarian aid convoys, and they consisted of documents relating to UNPROFOR convoys. Of those documents, on three occasions General Miletic signed, or it is attributed that General Miletic is having signed, as chief of operations and training. Of the documents that you reviewed in preparing your report, and the documents that you reviewed in preparing your testimony, on how many occasions did you see General Miletic's signature or signature block as attributed to anything other than standing in for the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a whole period in my work on this expert report that I devoted to trying to see, first of all, how the officers, primarily those from the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska, signed those document in order to be able to draw analogies. I then inspected some of the documents that pertained to General Miletic. I analysed the factual situation. I inspected the map, the file, in the personnel section which indicates clearly when somebody is standing in for or is not standing in for. I read the statement by General Manojlo, given by him, and on the basis of all that, I reached the conclusion that this was merely a bad way to sign a document. At the time when there was this replacement going on, I realised that all the documents that I saw were reports or notices. They are relatively urgent documents, and they have to be signed without undue delay by the person who is actually replacing another person. And I did not count the documents after that. I merely or, rather, I focussed exclusively on the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, let me qualify what I said before in respect of the number of documents. That was just for 1995, 587 documents I referred to, that was for the year 1995. But, in relation to what you've just said, it was part of your objective, for lack of a better term, to determine whether, in fact, General Miletic was functioning within the constraints of his position by establishment or whether he was performing functions that were outside that establishment; in other words, in the capacity of the Chief of Staff? That was part of your objective; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. You can read this in my report as well. When I established, based on all the parameters, that it was indeed the case, then I researched some other aspects, because this was not the only aspect of my expert work. The most important issue, that was what I relied on in order to establish that, was the link between the regulations regulating replacement, the factual situation, the contents of the regulations, and the position of his superior officer. His superior officer, if he had seen any other document, save for this report signed in this way, would have reacted differently because this would have meant that he also had been removed from his position. Because if somebody is standing in for him, then he cannot at the same time perform his duty. He would have he been removed from his position, he would not have been a commander, which means that he would have been chased out of his position. In any case, if Miletic had stood in for the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Army -- Republika Srpska Army, and that if the commander still performed his duty, that would mean the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Milovanovic Manojlo, had been removed from his duty, i.e., that he was no longer performing his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is relevant to determining the actual capacity in which General Miletic discharged his functional responsibilities to look at the capacity in which documents that are purportedly signed by him are attributed to him, whether that be chief of the Administration for Operations and Training or whether that be standing in for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. It would be relevant to see in what capacity he signed the documents. When I say "he," I mean General Miletic. And obviously, you would have to study all the documents and situations and everything that happened. I can say that he signed the document as the most senior officer in that place. The person who wanted to avoid the report being sent to Banja Luka and then being returned. It is very precise that in the capacity of the person that he was replacing at the moment he signed the document, having established by doing that he would not encroach his powers as replacing the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Given that that would be a relevant line of inquiry, that is, examining in what capacity these documents are attributed to him, whether it's in his capacity as per his establishment post or whether it is capacity as acting or standing in for the Chief of Staff, are you telling us that you have no idea as you testify here today how many times you saw in reviewing the documents General Miletic's name on a document that didn't say "standing in for the Chief of Staff"? You have no recollection of that? You can't estimate that for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not manage to note the third question. The first question was whether in his capacity as acting or standing in for the chief, he could not do that because in the establishment, the Chief of Staff did not have his deputy by establishment. And then you asked me your second question: He could not sign as standing in for the chief because he was never appointed to do stand in for the chief. And the third thing is something that we have already repeated several times, and you skipped over that. In his capacity as the most senior officer who at that moment in that place replaced the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Maybe something got lost in translation, but I will try again. Can you recall how many times in the documents that you reviewed you saw General Miletic's name associated with the position other than standing in for the Chief of Staff? Can you approximate that number?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have that statistic. And from the point of view from the expert report that I drafted and which had been given to me to do, this statistics would be -- would not be important. The statistics are important only to confirm some facts, and this is at least how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, one of the facts you were trying to confirm was that he wasn't actually standing in for the Chief of Staff; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I confirmed this fact by research rather than by statistics, and I believe that an expert report whose methodology is based on that does not require facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. In terms of evaluating the functional responsibilities of General Miletic, did you do that, first of all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I also told you what criteria I used to carry out the evaluation of his functional responsibilities. And I said from the outset that I never used that criteria because I knew only too well what I was doing and what was used in other works, and that functional responsibility of General Miletic was evaluated based on the rule on the powers of the corps commands, the rules on the powers of military districts, and so on and so forth. I evaluated that and studied functional responsibilities based on the functional responsibilities of the rank that he was a member of, which was a Main Staff which is in the same rank as a General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And those functional responsibilities would not entitle him to issue orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. His functional responsibilities would not allow him to issue orders, especially not orders to commands, units, and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 4158, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is an order that is signed by General Miletic standing in for the Chief of Staff. You could see on its face that it says "order." It's from the Main Staff, it's directed to the command of the airforce and anti-aircraft defence, as you can see. And it says: "Pursuant to the request for UNPROFOR command for urgent medical evacuation on 24 August, 1995, in a helicopter..." In quotes it says "seeking," "... aiming to regulate safe flying in the RS air-space, I hereby order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, before he answers, page 20, line 2, that question should be an answer, and there should be the removal of the question mark at the end, on line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document. Could it be scrolled up a little, please? Very well. Now I can see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see that it's an order; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 4159, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another document. It says at the top "Main Staff --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing against this line of questioning, but it would perhaps be good --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness to remove his headphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish the witness to remove his headphones or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if my learned colleague requests it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, could you remove yours headphones, please, and be patient with us. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against this line of questioning and these documents. There are surely a number of them, but perhaps we should come back to the period covered by the indictment. Certainly, we haven't explored or studied the functions of General Miletic in October 1995, and the indictment only ends at the end of August regarding General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, unless my colleagues wish me -- no. Okay. All right. We are fine with the question. General, thank you. Yes, let's proceed, please. If you could answer the question. Or, rather, I think he -- the question hasn't been put as yet, only part of it. You need to put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, this document is from the Main Staff, it has the number of 034-2818. 20th October 1995 is the date. And it says: "To the command of the Drina Corps, 67th infantry platoon, Main Staff headquarters administration and Main Staff traffic administration ..." And it concerns the cleaning up and sorting out of Srebrenica. And it's written "Order." You do see the word "order" written before you; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see that this document is also attributed to General Miletic as standing in for the Chief of Staff. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second document something has to be corrected in the translation. It is not the infantry platoon. PV stands for the communications regiment. That's what it should read. It is correct that both are orders; however, both orders were issued in compliance with the rules and regulations as to how an officer is replaced, and these regulations were valid, both valid at the time. These are two urgent orders. One is about helicopters and the rescue operation, and we commented upon this situation indirectly yesterday. And the second one is about the clean-up operation. At the moment when the orders were issued, they had to be signed by the most senior officer, and I assume that the most senior officer at the moment in the command post was General Miletic. If I had been there, I would have signed the two orders. I would not put "standing in for," but I would still have signed the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And why do you assume that the most senior officer at the command post must have been General Miletic? How can you make that assumption based on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't make that conclusion only based on this document, but on the entire context. I never look at a document in isolation but rather in its context. Bearing in mind the evaluation of his superior officer that he never acted in any other way, this was a good enough indicator for me that at that moment in the main base -- in the base command post there was nobody but General Miletic. And it can be seen from all the other parts that he was not in the command post, only when he was in Bosnia and Herzegovina discounting some other cases, for example, once when he was assigned to go on a mission, the whole context and the whole situation and the fact that these are documents that have nothing to do with the use of any units, but, rather, humanitarian aid and assistance extended to the population and the city. I believe that this was enough to establish the context and that all this was in compliance with the regulations and rule that were in effect in Republika Srpska at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Couldn't you just as easily conclude that he was standing in for the Chief of Staff and that's why he issued the order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analogy which is now offered would have been detrimental for the Army Republika Srpska. It would be disastrous. No single corps command would allow for somebody to order him if he was not standing in for the chief but only impersonating somebody who was standing in for the chief. The Chief of Staff would not allow such a person to issue orders and make decisions. Knowing General Miletic and his professional career and having read official evaluations offered by others, since we did not serve together, I concluded that this is a huge difference. Basing your analogy on humanitarian aid and saying that he also issued combat orders would not make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 4055, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, what you have before you -- what you have before you is a document that's dated 10 March 1995, and it concerns convoys. In particular, in this document, if we go to page 2 of the B/C/S, you can see that it's type-signed standing in for the Chief of Staff, Colonel Miletic. Now, if we go to the first page again of the B/C/S, the document is dated 10th March, 1995. It is directed to the command of Drina Corps. And in its first sentence it reads: "Please be advised that we approved the weekly plan of distribution of humanitarian assistance from Belgrade for Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period from 11 March till 17 March 1995." Now, in a previous document that was shown to you, I asked you about what was the necessary of the Main Staff indicating an approval of humanitarian aid that had already been approved? You said "It couldn't hurt." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was more complex, you simplified it. But I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't need you to repeat it. I just want to know if you remember that part of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember in a much more precise way than you used to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this particular document you can see that it says that "We approved the weekly plan of distribution of humanitarian assistance from Belgrade for Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then it says in the following sentence: "We reduced the plan for the enclaves in number of vehicles and the transport of fuel is not committed. Despite the information on restrictions we submitted to the coordinating body for humanitarian aid. We expect the UNHCR shall try to bring fuel into the enclaves which has to be prevented." You see that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the bottom of the page in English, and we go to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, you look in the paragraph in the B/C/S designated 16.03.95. In English you can see there is a remark, and it indicates: "Regarding medicine for Srebrenica approved for 14 March 1995, we shall send to the command of the Drina Corps a separate list of medicine once we coordinate." Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this context is it appropriate for the Main Staff to reduce the amount of the planned convoy or humanitarian aid for the enclaves even though it's already been approved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw the correspondence between the coordination body and the Main Staff. If Main Staff as a professional organ in the sytem of the functioning of humanitarian aid provided its position and view points as to what humanitarian aid could be used in combat against the Army Republika Srpska. And also the Main Staff by the way of the functioning of the -- of humanitarian aid could also provide its proposals for something to be reduced. When such a proposal for reduction was given, it always informed, as you can see here, and the coordination body could reject that proposal or adopt it. Hence, the research of the relationship between the Main Staff and the coordination body is not something that I did in detail, but as far as I could see, they did not have many problems between themselves. They had other problems that needed to be discussed, and they did indeed discuss them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see that this document, in particular, is type-signed by Colonel Miletic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the typed block signature. As I can see, this was sent by way of teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 4062, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is a similar document. It is dated 30 June 1995. It's from the Main Staff, Republika Srpska. It's directed to the command of the Drina Corps. And it leads as follows, well, it reads and leads as follows: "Please be advised that we agree with realisation of authorisation of the coordinating body for humanitarian aid to the Republika Srpska," and it gives a number 1582-HCR-867, "related to the weekly plan of the Belgrade UNHCR as follows." And you can see under 4 July there is a remark. And it indicates, "We did not approve one more truck within this convoy with school supplies." Now, is this consistent with your understanding of the Main Staff role vis-a-vis the coordinating body for humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should research this part in detail because there is also another part, and that is once bitten, twice shy. Personally when I look at this whole thing, I don't see a reason for that; however, if you were to study the context of what was done and how things were done, then one could say that they overstepped their authorities, or one could say that for some reason this was done. The elements do not suffice for me to conclude what was done and why things were done the way they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You do see at the bottom of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just scroll down in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that that is also type-signed, General Radivoje Miletic standing in for the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both documents were sent by teleprinter. They are both notices or notifications. And both documents carry the signature block that we can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And both documents actually restrict pre-approved humanitarian aid, that's true too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both documents are notifications indicating that the Main Staff of the VRS and the coordination body are to have a coordination meeting about restricting humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, General. I think the documents speak for themselves. You did in your report cover the area of humanitarian aid; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of humanitarian aid, as concerns the enclaves, you did evaluate what the humanitarian condition of the enclaves were between, say, January and July of 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So it's fair to say in your evaluation of the humanitarian condition of the enclaves during that period that you concluded - and you'll correct me if I'm wrong - that there was no specific indication of a deteriorating humanitarian condition; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of stating this in such uncertain terms anywhere. I made some comments about humanitarian aid in ten -- or, rather, eight paragraphs, all told, and I made my conclusions on the basis of what I had gone through. And since the topic was not something that was -- I was to cover in my analysis, I never put this in, but I did state that I found in some documents instances that humanitarian aid -- there were abuses of humanitarian aid effort, and I indicated this was a big problem, the abuse of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So you never actually evaluated what the condition of what the -- what the humanitarian condition was during the period of time that you were actually considering what General Miletic's role was in the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not analyse this in detail. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I show you 65 ter 4124.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During your testimony, one of the things that you mentioned was you -- was that people that were in the enclaves expressed their wish to leave. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in so many words. I merely stated on the basis of the reports that I read from the UN Secretary-General and the documents that I read originating from the Main Staff of the BH army, the reports from the security organ of the 2nd Corps of the BH army, on the basis of the reports -- of the commanders in Srebrenica and Zepa and on the basis of the local leaders that there was always this tension present among the population that they actually wanted to leave the enclave. I did not have a personal view, and I could not form a personal view because I was not there, so this was merely stating some facts that are based on what I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. This document is an UNPROFOR office of civil affairs document. It's a weekly situation report covering the period of 26 February to 4 March 1995. What I'd like to do is to refer you to page 5 of this document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could go down the page to number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Number 15 reads "Srebrenica supplies." And it reads as follows: "After the UNPROFOR troops in Srebrenica literally ran out of food (they consumed their last combat rations on 3 March) the BSA finally agreed today after several prior refusals to law the troops resupply. The BSA explaining that they have no objection to food deliveries, only to fuel, continue to refuse delivery of fuel to Srebrenica, and they continue to refuse medical supplies into the three enclaves." Were you aware of these facts at the time you were drafting your report or in preparation for drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned several times, Your Honours, that I never put in anything that is based on just one document. And I never look at documents in isolation. This is not in line with the methodology that I decided to use in the drafting of my report. The report that I see in front of me, I think I have seen it before. I read it in the context of many other reports and in the context of the reports indicating that humanitarian aid was used to reward and pay fighters in where humanitarian aid was used to provide logistics support to the 28th Division. And I decided that this area should be explored very carefully, lest there should be any such manipulations based on excerpts taken from -- out of the context. Since General Miletic was not part of the system whereby proposals were drafted and decisions were made in the area of humanitarian aid, I ceased researching this area in detail. And I am only saying that this should be viewed within its context.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 4125, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a cable that is directed to Annan, United Nations New York. It is dated 22 March 1995, and I am going to refer you, specifically, to paragraph number 3 of this document. It reads, in the first sentence: "UNHCR reports that they have managed to get medical supplies into Gorazde and Srebrenica for the first time since November 1994." Were you aware of that fact in the context of drafting your report or preparing to testify? And I ask you this because you've talked a lot about abuses that have occurred in the process, justification for the restriction of fuel, and justification for the imposition of restrictions as regards the inspection of convoys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I hope I'm not pedantic, but I think that my learned friend should say "assertion" rather than "fact."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Josse is right. Mr. Vanderpuye, you said, page 31, line 1: "Were you aware of the fact ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware of what was asserted in this document? I hope that satisfies my colleague. Are you aware of what is reported in this document at the time that you prepared your report to testify in this case? And I ask you for reasons that I've indicated before and also to the extent that you've said that there is no indication that you've come across that -- supporting the notion that life was made unbearable for the inhabitants of these enclaves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never found any justification, and I always insisted that things should be looked at in their context, I constantly insisted. And it is my position throughout this report that I am studying facts and checking assertions. And on the basis of having checked the assertions and obtaining the facts, I draw my conclusions. If I were to say that each action was justified, and if I were unable to support that with facts, I would not be a serious scholar. And, Your Honours, I never did that. I never did any of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question is were you aware of what's asserted; that is, that the UNHCR managed to get medical supplies into Gorazde and Srebrenica for the first time since 1994 on or around 22nd March 1995 when this report is dated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware of this assertion, of this claim. I never saw it; I never read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 4126, please. This is another cable. It's dated 18 April, 1995, addressed to Mr. Annan. If we could go to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At item number 4 it reads: "The following additional information further clarifies the situation." A, it says: "Srebrenica, has been using UNHCR stocks of diesel of which 38.4 cubic metres have been used so far. The battalion reduced consumption rates some weeks ago to 3.5 cubic metres per day and has now cut consumption to 1.5 cubic metres per day. Strict limitations have been placed on the use of vehicles and generators. The operational effects have resulted in a much reduced patrolling programme." For Zepa under C it reads: "There is no vehicle controlling in Zepa, and the company is using wood for cooking and candles for light." Were you aware of the existence of those circumstances in April of 1995 as is reported in this document in the preparation of your report or in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this and for a very simple reason. For me to be aware of the document and for me to be able to use a document in drafting my expert report, the document had to have been translated. Since my knowledge or, rather, lack of knowledge of English makes it impossible for me to study documents that had not been translated. In order to be able to form an opinion at the time or now, we need to look at claims made by both sides, and then those facts and claims have to be checked and then conclusions can be reached. Now, I am faced with the plethora of claims made by one side, and I was able to look at claims both about the abuse of humanitarian aid and the lack of humanitarian aid. But since this was not a topic that I was researching, I did not pay much attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break. I would appreciate it if we can take it now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. We will have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, how much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have about ten documents to go through with the witness. They are similar to this document. I don't anticipate it will be how much longer than how -- on average how long it's been going with each of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have 65 ter 4130, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is an UNPROFOR document. It's from the office of civil affairs. It's a weekly situation report indicating the week of 8 through 15 May 1995, and it's dated 15 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Excuse me, under item 10 it reads as follows: "Serbs allow some UNHCR convoys into the eastern enclaves of Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica, but continue to deny UNPROFOR resupplies creating critical conditions for the troops. The Serbs' contention is that so long as they suffer under international sanctions, they will impose the same predicament on Bosnian areas over which they have leverage." Now, sir, this document and the other documents that I have shown you from the UN, UNHCR, it's the Prosecution's position that these documents show that Directive 7 is alive. It was not invalidated by Directive 7/1, particularly in respect of making life unbearable and in respect of accomplishing that through the restrictive use of permits. Now, having looked at this and having had an opportunity to consider the report as I've just read it to you, does this, in your opinion -- does this, in your opinion, contradict what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is very important to note that this is not a topic of Directive 7 or Directive 7/1. The scope of the directive can only be seen on the basis of the tasks issued to the units. Humanitarian aid was operational as was the supply of units and irritation of UNPROFOR units. It was within the remit of the coordination body and the Main Staff. And it is obvious that neither Directive 7 nor Directive 7/1 were sent to the coordination body and to the Main Staff, and it did not entail any tasks issued to them. And we can see here that there are problems with supply lines for UNPROFOR, and we can see on the basis of a number of assertions that UNPROFOR was operating outside of its mandate. And by researching both topics, then one can get a full picture and see what is cause and what is consequence. At any rate, we can see this assertion here, but it needs to be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 4132 in e-court, please. And if we could go to the bottom of the page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another UNPROFOR document. It is dated 1st June 1995. And at the bottom of this page you can see it reads: "The most critical situation with the food is in Gorazde and Zepa," and it says "UKRKOY," "... due to the blockade of these pockets by the BSA, there is no opportunity to resupply." Now, were you aware of this, what is represented in this particular document at the time of drafting your report and -- well, let me ask you that first. Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this document. If it was translated and if it was in the database of the translated documents, then I probably would have been aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about the circumstances about which it speaks, that is, the inability to resupply UNPROFOR troops?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about this whole set of circumstances, and I knew of a document indicating that immediately before that a large quantity of humanitarian aid was given by way of logistics support to the 28th Division. So I knew about this assertion and about the facts that I saw from a document originating from the local authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me take you to 65 ter 4133. It's dated 4 June, 1995. And it's also an UNPROFOR weekly situation report covering the period of 29 May through 4 June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not an objection. I would just like to inform the Chamber about the fact that the series of documents which is currently being presented to the witness are documents which were disclosed to the Defence teams on the 30th [as interpreted] of January of this year, so the witness can't have seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's what I thought you had said, actually, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 -- 5 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Under item 14 it reads that: "The food situation is at an unsatisfactorily level as well. Serbs had reassured all the humanitarian agencies to continue their normal activities. However, with the current security situation and the lack of UNPROFOR escorts for convoys, UNHCR decided to suspend its convoys. UNHCR has 370 tonnes of food at the airport. Since 3 June UNPROFOR has been protecting UNHCR convoys to cart the food from the airport to the city." If we go down to item 17, we see "Situation in the Enclaves," and it reads: "Limited amounts of humanitarian assistance through convoys reached Tuzla during the reporting period. All other enclaves did not receive their scheduled supplies. Should the present state of affairs persist, the enclaves which depend entirely on humanitarian assistance will suffer tremendously." Sir, it's the Prosecution's position that this is evidence of the fact that Directive 7 was not invalidated. It is evidence of the fact that the population in the enclaves was made to suffer unbearable conditions of life. And it is the position of the Prosecution that that was -- that was inflicted upon them by restrictive use of permits as is indicated in Directive 7 and that that contradicts your explanation that Directive 7/1 invalidated Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, despite all my best efforts to understand this question, it is a fact that this is not a fact. It's a claim. That's number 1. Number 2. What I said at the time and what I am saying now, your position that the directive is what it is, this is your position, and I told you something that is well known throughout the world, what kind of a document a directive is and to whom it is addressed as a document. What is the task that is contained in a directive, and who is assigned this task? Any analogy stating that a directive is an executive document cannot be justified by anything that I found in any of my analyses, and I also never said that Directive 7/1 abolished Directive 7. I clearly specified what paragraphs and what items -- what units. I maintain that it is a delusion to say that the directive regulates the field of humanitarian aid. There are appropriate documents enacted by the Republika Srpska. There is a specific document issued by the army. And this was regulated in a completely different manner. In order to verify this, for instance, this report by UNPROFOR, it would be a good idea to give me the whole of the report, and then we could see whether the report deals with all the elements in an appropriate manner, whether the report deals with the exchange of intelligence, whether it deals with a number of other issues that were their mission. I am not saying "yes," and I am not saying "no." I am only saying that this has nothing to do with Directive number 7, and any efforts to link any directive or any military order with what we see here amounts to speculation, and this is inappropriate for any military.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the clarification of the record, Mr. President, the document 4133 that I've just used with the expert was disclosed on 23rd January, 2008. This next document, 4136, I'd like to have in e-court as well, was also disclosed on 23rd January, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, this is another document, also a similar document. It indicates in the top left corner, UNPROFOR communications. It is addressed to Mr. Annan, and it is dated 14 June 1995. In the second point -- second paragraph, if we could page down a little bit, it reads as follows: "None of the UNHCR convoys to the enclaves have received clearances. The Srebrenica convoy has been cancelled. The Sarajevo convoy has not left Zenica. The BSA are demanding a 50/50 share of the aid to which UNHCR will not agree. The UNPF resupply convoys have suffered a similar fate. The two convoys to Gorazde were blocked by the BSA and have returned to Sarajevo. The convoy scheduled to depart from Zagreb for Sarajevo has not yet received clearance. Were you aware, as I've said before, during the drafting of your report in preparation of your testimony of the circumstances that are described in this particular passage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the context and the circumstances prevailing with regard to Republika Srpska. And in Republika Srpska, I was aware of the entire context that you have just spoken about. I was aware of the overall context of the blockade of the entire state. I was aware of the entire context of misuse. And I knew of the context that bans were introduced, and the research will show that some bans were justified and some were not. This is an entirely different topic, and this different topic has to be over-viewed and analysed in detail rather than, by the way, by extracting some segments and sentences from their context. Initially, when I first started working, when I reviewing all the elements before I moved on to the concrete part, I also analysed the humanitarian aid that was delivered, oscillations, the causes and consequences between the quantity of humanitarian aid and the number of population, the quantity of help, the number of units, the frequency of humanitarian aid and the number of units, the rotation of forces, and so on and so forth. When I saw that this goes beyond my commission, I dropped that part and this part remained as separated, but it serves as the good basis of information pointing to the fact that this part requires a lot of work and a lot of future research.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 4138. For the record, this was also disclosed on 23rd January, 2008. This cable concerns daily reporting. It is dated 20th June 1995. It's addressed to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on the second page of this document - if we could turn to that please - at point five it indicates or reads as follows: "Problems with convoys, both logistics, resupply, and UNHCR continue in my parts of the UNPROFOR AOR. The 56 truck convoy bound for the eastern enclaves arrived in Belgrade yesterday. However, the BSA has cut the number of trucks from 56 to 23, has cut the amount of food by 50 per cent and the amount of fuel by 70 per cent, has rejected the passage of two ambulances needed for UN troops, and has insisted that those personnel travelling with the convoy to the enclaves must also depart with it, though no one else may, in other words, preventing any troop rotation or reinforcement." It indicates: "Attached is a summary of the material requested for the convoy and the material approved by the BSA. A UNHCR convoy destined for Gorazde and given approval by Pale has been stopped and is now held-up 15 kilometres short of the enclave." And the last sentence of this paragraph will read as follows: "UNMOs in Srebrenica and Gorazde have not been able to rotate for more than 60 days. Repeated requests for their rotation have been refused by the BSA." In light of the other documents that I've shown you and in light of the Prosecution's position as I've stated to you, it is the case that this document also contradicts your assessment of the effect of Directive 7/1?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this document that you have just shown and looking at the whole collection that I've been provided with, I am very concerned that not having seen anywhere that Mr. Kofi Annan was ever informed about the misuse of humanitarian aid. You have never shown me a document. While I was doing my research I found over 35 per cent, a clearly defined procedure of the functioning of UNPROFOR with the army and the timely notification of the rotation of the forces and the -- at that moment of the number of -- the research documents that in 30 per cent of cases, the notifications were belated. The statement that this is a directly related to Directive number 7 at first was likely that the goal and the intention of the directive was not well understood, that its functioning was not well understood, as well, how it is implemented now. I see that this is not due to the lack of understanding, but the claim that is not in consistency with any military doctrine or any state in the world which has a serious military.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 4054, please. Thank you. For the record, this document was also disclosed on 14 March 2008. If we could go to page 2 of this document, it is dated 7 July 1995. It is an UN cable directed to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From page 2 at point 4 it reads as follows, General: "The first UNHCR convoy since 20 May arrived in Gorazde yesterday with 78 metric tonnes of flour, beans, salt, and oil. An UNHCR convoy of 56 metric tonnes was also successful in gaining access to Zepa. The UNPROFOR leave and rotation convoy to Gorazde stopped at Rogatica on the grounds that its clearance was no longer valid, will try to re-enter -- will try to enter the pocket today. Another UNPROFOR convoy bound for Srebrenica returned to Belgrade after having been obstructed by the BSA. UNHCR was targeted twice yesterday and BH or convoy being escorted by PakBat around Ribnica came under BSA artillery fire." Now, were you aware of the circumstances involving he obstruction of the rotation of UNPROFOR troops or convoys bound for the enclaves by the BSA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please be shown the first page of the document? Thank you. As I'm reading this document and as I'm reading these claims, I can't escape the impression that although this is about UNPROFOR, it is still beyond UNPROFOR. A very important statement that impacts my view is the fact that a reference is here to the BCS, something that did not exist, and that is the army of Bosnian Serbs. I knew that UNPROFOR knew very precisely that it was VRS rather than the BSA. My impression is that the document was drafted by somebody else. Second of all, I can see here some very precise data, and that's why I am taken by surprise. Not to see in this document that the humanitarian aid and the logistics of the DutchBat provided logistical support to the 28th Division. There is very precise document which you have and on which the head of the local administration -- administration in Srebrenica reported on. I am not doubting any of this, however, the facts in these documents and the claims in these documents I would check in a context, I would put them in a context, and then, only then, would I be able and would I be willing to provide my concrete conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it your opinion, General, that the restriction of troop rotations is an appropriate response to the violation of some convoy regulation or rule? Is that your opinion, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not my opinion. However, I can't say anything before I see the whole. Only then would I be able to state that the restriction was the only possible answer at a certain point in time. But even if that was the case, even if this was the only possible answer, this was something that the state bodies and the military were in charge of, and it -- this has nothing to do with what you are saying, and you are saying that this was done to Directive number 7 or Directive number 7/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I want to make sure in my mind that we are understanding the same thing by "restriction of troop rotations," as we have it in the transcript. What do you mean by that, "restriction of troop rotations"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It relates to the UNMOs that were the subject of the previous document, and it also relates to the obstruction of the UNPROFOR convoys that had returned to Belgrade in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And is that the way you understood it, General, when you gave your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I understood things even in a more complex manner. All the rotations and all the enforcements, yes, absolutely in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 4142, please, in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document as you can see in the top right hand corner is stamped "UNMO headquarters." It is a cable from UNMO headquarters UNPROFOR Sarajevo to UNMO headquarters Zagreb, and it's dated 8 July, 1995. And under item number 1, if we can page down and make it easier for everyone to see, it talks about the number and status of inhabitants, and it regards the food situation in Srebrenica, status for food to the civilian population. And it reads, under item 1: "Total population, 42.000; item B, 85 per cent of those -- or 85 percent were refugees or displaced persons, 20 per cent being locals." And it says: "Status Food." Under item 2, "UNHCR Stock:" "The food stock in the UNHCR warehouse is almost zero. There is not even sufficient stock to run the social kitchens to provide one meal a day for the most vulnerable." Under item B, that is, point 2: "Estimated private stock on the average may last for not more than a couple of days providing for one or at most two meals a day per person." It says, under item C, "NGO stock, MSF, Medecins Sans Frontieres:" "The supplies of MSF are very limited and depending on the number of the wounded from the ongoing shelling, this may last for an approximated two to four weeks." If we go to page 2 of this document, under item 3 -- remarks under item 3, and item 3 deals with UNHCR planned deliveries of food. It says: "If the UNHCR planned convoys (i.e. three convoys per week) were implemented, this would have served barely about 65 per cent of the needs of the entire population; however, with the present rate of delivery, less than 25 per cent of the needs is being met." Now, sir when you prepared your report and when you evaluated the information in order to do that to testify, were you aware of this information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is dated 8 July. If I am not mistaken, 8 July 1995. I have not seen this particular one. However, in the first sentence, if we can go back to the previous page, please, I believe that this is not the estimate of the population but the exact number of the population. It says here the number and status of the population, the total number, not the evaluation of the total number. If I am mistaken, I apologise. I was aware of this and such evaluations; however, I also knew and I would like to compare the reports of the local administration whose estimates were lower, but they provided higher numbers in order to obtain more humanitarian aid, more higher quantity thereof. And I can see here that when it comes to the number of the population, this comprises the 28th Division, which is a respectable force, but it does not fall under the entitlement to humanitarian aid. And it comprises over 20 per cent of the total figure, here. I also know that in the interval after that, 600 combatants of the 28th Division were engaged, and they were paid in flour and other type of humanitarian aid. I know that some other types of humanitarian aid were sent to this division, and I know that a few days later the depots were broken in and a lot of humanitarian aid was stolen. And when we put all the pieces of that puzzle together, then I can tell you exactly what facts are credible. I could be able to tell you what the cause and the consequences are. As things stand now, I can say that I am aware of all this, but I find it very unusual that no single report deals with the factual situation as it was on the ground at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, General. Well, you have to view all of these things in context, I guess, is that your point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these UN documents, as I've put them to you, in fact put the events on the ground in context.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. If we look at them as a whole. If we look at the causes and consequences and not in this way. If we only extract some reports from them, some excerpts from them, and we do not provide the view from the other side. If that's how we wish to proceed, then we do not have a context.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
