utterances.text: All right. And you're here to put the perspective of the other side to the Trial Chamber; is that right? Is that how you view your role, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unlike some other things that were prepared, in my documents I -- or, rather, in my expert report I used documents produced by both the warring parties, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Army Republika Srpska. I also used documents produced by UNPROFOR that I was privy to. I used databases and procedures as they were defined in the Army of Republika Srpska and how they are defined in other militaries, and in NATO members. I provided the true causal and consequential relationship. And if you look at my expert report, I put forth some claims that have never been put forth so far which are not very professional, and they are very problematic for the Army Republika Srpska. I looked at the situation in their dynamics, because in combat actions, there are always two sides present.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could 65 ter 4145, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document is entitled "Information Notes," it is published by the UNHCR. I should point out that a similar document was put to a different witness by the Miletic Defence. And I want to show you, if I could, page 19 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, its dated July 1995. All right. I think we have to go one more page, I'm sorry. I think 18, I guess -- I mean, sorry, 20 I think. One more. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What this shows, General, is the food delivery targets and the food delivery to the eastern enclaves. You can see at the top it says -- I'll read it to you. It says "Aid to Bosnian enclaves," and in particular. I'd focus your attention to Srebrenica and Zepa. Those are the two right columns. In June of 1995 it indicates that 230 metric tonnes in four convoys went to Srebrenica. And if we go down -- well, before I get to that, it also shows 50 metric tonnes of aid went to Zepa in one convoy. That's for the month of June. If we could go down to the bottom of the page, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could maybe blow up the right hand corner, that would be -- a little bit more. That's great.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the right hand corner - I'll read it to you - it says: "Note: The June 1995 food delivery target for Bihac was 1.000 metric tonnes; Gorazde, 772 metric tonnes; Srebrenica, 678 metric tonnes; and Zepa, 160 metric tonnes." That was the target. As you can see from this document in June 1995 Srebrenica was 230 metric tonnes which is about a third of the target. Zepa was 50 metric tonnes, about roughly the same, about a third of the intended target. Where you can also see -- and I have to go to a different page for this. But before I do, firstly, were you aware that these targets were so wilfully not met, the intended aid targets were so reduced from what was expected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, when I started working I followed humanitarian aid. I studied Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. I had similar information and data; however, when I learned from the local authorities how many inhabitants there were in really -- and how many was planned for humanitarian aid, then my diagrams assumed a total different character. If the ratio -- I am sorry that I have not seen this document before. If I could study this, then I would look at the plan; I would look at the starting parameters for planning; I would look at the true planning parameters. And then I believe that the graph representation would look entirely different. I am aware of the problem. I know that this has to be studied, but I know that the whole thing represented in this unilateral way can only lead to confusion and a false impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 7, please, of this same document. It should be an ERN ending 3198. All right. If we could go down. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the left-hand side it reads: "Humanitarian situation in the eastern enclaves. "The situation in the eastern enclaves where only 17 per cent of the overall monthly aid delivery target was met in June is also very serious." It talks about: "No convoy could reach Gorazde last month as a result of obstructions by the Bosnian Serbs. The food situation became critical as household reserves dwindled due to the long interruption in aid distribution. The local authorities had to resort to collecting wheat grain from surrounding villages for distribution to vulnerable cases in the town." Further down in this document it talks about Zepa, and it says: "Zepa also faced serious humanitarian access problems. There were no convoys for a four-week period until one was able to reach the enclave on 21 June. "There is a dramatic humanitarian situation developing in Srebrenica at the time of writing this report. The BSA initiated an attack on the pocket on 8/9 July and captured 30 Dutch peacekeepers there. On 10 July the UN warned the BSA to halt their advance or face NATO retaliation." Now, in terms of the humanitarian situation as described concerning Zepa, Gorazde, and Srebrenica, were you aware of those -- of what the fact -- what the report indicates here, the information that the report contains at the time of drafting your report or in preparing to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this information. I studied this information. And I particularly studied what is mentioned here under the titles "Obstruction." I am surprised that this report does not show any self-criticism. I am astounded that this report doesn't say in any place -- or maybe it does, but you have given me just excerpts, that there was obstruction in the request for humanitarian aid, in the planning of humanitarian aid, in the fact that in the request for humanitarian aid, one thing is represented and the situation on the ground is entirely different. If we were to analyse all this, then we would probably redistribute this problem of obstruction in a different way, and I'm afraid that we could find consequences in a different place, which would not suit us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could show you 65 ter 4146, please. This is a similar document, it's actually the same author. And if we could go to, I think it's going to be page 21 in this document. It's ERN ending 3182.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a very similar chart to what I showed you before except that it includes the figures for July 1995. In respect of Srebrenica and Zepa respectively, we have 88 metric tonnes of aid going in and two convoys in Zepa 56. If we go down to the bottom of this page, all the way down, you can see in the note what the targets are. And in this case it indicates that the Srebrenica -- the target for Srebrenica was 720 metric tonnes, of which 88 were met, and in Zepa 168 metric tonnes of which 56 were met. I take it, sir, that you weren't aware of this information either at the time of either drafting your report or preparing to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have these reports at my disposal, and now I wouldn't be in a position to claim that I didn't have them on the CD either, but if they were among the documents, they were not translated, and I don't know in what context. You are now pointing me to July 1995, if I am not mistaken, which those tables refer to because the month of July 1995 -- well, I don't know what was the basis for the plans and needs presented here by this institution, what -- who the aid was supposed to reach. So the whole purpose of this document that pertains to July 1995 and the situation on the field, apart from the oscillations that are presented here, well, I can't see any essential purpose of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me direct you to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 4161.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you should have in front of you is a Drina Corps document. It's addressed to Colonel Popovic as it reads in the English translation. And it is a request indicated, delivery of requirements for the Ukraine units deployed in Zepa. Have you seen this document before, first of all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know who Colonel Popovic is or who Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is within the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know who this refers to because I am not that familiar with the persons who were in the Drina Corps, and that is why I find it strange the way this document is drafted. I can't see the date. I don't know what organ this pertains to, and I can't see the whole of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your expertise, is there any particular reason why a document listing items concerning the delivering of requirements for Ukraine unit in Zepa would be addressed to a security officer in the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see -- well, I didn't study this document, and I can't see any particular rational reason except if the military police units provided security or were present in the field. And then, in that manner, this document was the basis for allowing a convoy through. I can't see any other reasonable reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And finally in respect of your analysis of General Miletic's signature in the context of standing in for the Chief of Staff, were you aware that General Miletic, at that time Colonel Miletic, signed in signature block for the Chief of Staff as early as 1993, standing in for the Chief of Staff as early as 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, but I don't want to be speaking off the top of high head here. The chief of the administration, General Miletic, may have been there from August 1993, the chief of the Administration for Operations and Training. And in line -- if we look at the dynamics of the operations that ensued and the position that General Miletic held, the fact that he was at the basic command post, the fact that the greatest fluctuation in combat is the flow of information, reports, and other documents, auxiliary documents that I was talking about, this figure does not come as a surprise. And I think that one could expect even a greater number of document. The frequency of information -- informations report, notifications is huge. It's a vast number of documents when you have a combat situation, so I expected this kind of figure. I didn't have it, but I expected the figure to be something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I have just one document I would like show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am going to need the ELMO for this, Mr. President. We will put this into e-court under 65 ter 4219. If we could just go to the top of the page so we can see what we are looking at here. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a Main Staff document. It has the date. It's above -- if we can move up to we can see it. It's dated 8th October, 1993. And the number of the document is 17/231-517. And it's directed to the Drina Corps command; that's right, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could just go to the next page. Okay. And we can see from the signature here that this is standing in for the Chief of Staff is, type-signed, Radivoje Miletic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That's all I wanted to establish. And you are aware, of course, that these documents existed, these type-signed documents of Colonel Miletic, General Miletic, right up through 1995 as standing in for the Chief of Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my colleague clarify his position? Is he saying that General Miletic, who at the time was Colonel Miletic, was the representative of the staff during this entire period -- representative of the Chief of Staff, rather?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I am not saying that at all. I think my question is very clear, that there are documents like that that exist that go right from 1993 right up to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You are aware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the document that you've now put in front of me, first of all we can see clearly the context, and I will share it with you. First of all you said "stand in for," and I say he never stood in for; whereas, the fact that it's written here on this document, it's a different matter. Had he been standing in for all -- throughout this time it would is been a world record in standing in for. And since you said that he did not stand in for, and since you made documents in various ways, then out of the ten orders to stand in for, there would be at least one valid order to that effect, and we would be able to see it here. The Chief of Staff himself stated that he had never been prevented from performing his duties, so nobody could have stood in for him. This document probably indicates the following: That at the point in time when this information, this notice had to be sent out - because this is the kind of document that we are talking about - that at the basic command post General Miletic was the senior officer, at the time he was a colonel, and as the most senior officer he signed this notice so that it could be sent out lest they should wait for the Chief of Staff to return from wherever he was. So it is one of the consistent documents regulating the replacement in an appropriate manner. The fact that the Chief of Staff, General Manojlo, in May 1995 in his official personnel assessment clearly indicated that he never did anything outside of what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And in your estimation there is nothing unusual about that document, and it does in fact say on it, that Colonel Miletic is standing in for the Chief of Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this again, but since I have been cautioned I have to explain it in a different may. In my opinion I am quite precise. When I say in this case Colonel Miletic, later General Miletic, carried out the standing in for, or, rather, replacing, carried out the replacing in line with all the rules, in line with the position taken by his superior, in line with the usual practice, and what I said in my report, I believe that this signature block was a clumsy solution. That's the least I can say. And who was responsible for this clumsy solution? It was as much General Manojlo Milovanovic and Colonel Miletic who actually came up with it. They shared the responsibility for that. But standing in for was done exclusively in line with the regulations. The two orders that you produced had to do with humanitarian aid and some emergency situations, and it is strange that you're now showing them as something that is not quite in line with the real situation of standing in for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, my question is limited to the document, just the document that is sitting right there next to you in your right hand. It says "Standing in for the Chief of Staff." That's what it says; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... dated 1993, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it doesn't look strange to you or unusual to you in any respect, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at the contents that you are skipping here, no, it doesn't look strange at all. It looks to be extremely in line with the rules, that he's acting in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness should take off his earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, once more you have to be patient with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I rise now because we have an application to further cross-examine the witness. Let me make it clear it will be Mr. Krgovic who will carry that cross-examine out consistent with how we proceeded before. There are two issues that we wish to address in that cross-examination. The first is the New York Times article that was put to the witness, P4201; and the second issue, relates to the ICRC documents that were put to the witness, basically P4156 and P157. Mr. Krgovic estimates that his further cross-examination would take 15 to 20 minutes. There are, I think, three or four documents on a list that we have available for distribution. We thought it fair to do this now before Madam Fauveau carries out her re-examination of the witness. And it's our submission that these are areas that we really could not have anticipated the Prosecution asking the witness about, and we should be allowed to ask the witness further questions in relation to those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to comment, Ms. Fauveau, and Mr. Vanderpuye? Ms. Fauveau first. Do you object to further cross-examination? No. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we take no position on Mr. Josse's application --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, however, I want to hear what he cross-examines on, because if he opens a new door, I anticipate we will make an application to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Fauveau, I think can start with her redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's do it this way. Mr. Krgovic, usually we ask for the questions beforehand, before we decide, but having discussed very briefly I think we can trust in your discretion and allow you to go ahead. Try to be as brief as possible, please. And Madam Fauveau, how much your redirect -- depending, of course, what is going to happen now. But how much do you anticipate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if my colleague requires 15 to 20 minutes, I will do my utmost to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Krgovic. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon again, Mr. Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, the Prosecutor -- well, General, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, the Prosecutor showed you an article from the New York Times written by a John Burns a journalist, dated the spring of 1993 which you characterized as a propaganda pamphlet. And in my opinion he speaks bad words about Serbs and about General Gvero. Do you know that this journalist John Burns is quite well known for having used the New York Times in the spring of 1993 to launch a story about how two Serb soldiers killed two Muslim twins and how these men were then sentenced to death by the Muslim authorities, it was Hara [phoen] case. And then it turned out that the twins were found to be alive at a later date. And the New York Times, several years later, had to publish a denial of this story.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of this case. I wasn't aware of the fact that this is the same journalist. And I know why in May 1995 this story was published because it was there to cover up the responsibility of those who were really responsible for what happened in Zepa when it was turned into an enclave to cover up the false reporting and many other things and to draw the attention of the world public to something that didn't really exist. I did not do any research into the facts, but I know very well what the key problem was in Eastern Bosnia in May 1995. And any other attempt to derail, to destroy, to turn it into something else, is an effort to coverup.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are referring to 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1993, I'm sorry. This is when this story was published, the one that we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, the Prosecutor asked you a series of questions about the meetings between the Serb side and UNPROFOR representatives and the ICRC representatives showing you, among other documents, a report from a meeting where mention is made about General Gvero being in attendance. Do you personally know that General Gvero did, in fact, attend this meeting on the 16th of June? I am not talking about what you saw in the document but what you know, yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all -- and this is completely outside the scope of the cross-examination, and it doesn't call for an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How does this fit in with what Mr. Josse described to us as going to be your further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is another document of the ICRC which I would like to show to this witness which indicates that up until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show the document and ask him the question, the pertinent question. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 6D320. Could we see the bottom half of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, you see here, it's a request from the ICRC to the state committee for cooperation with international organisations, the coordination body.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's for the evacuation of the wounded. The date is the 16th of July, 1995. It is precisely what the document was about, the document that the Prosecutor asked you about. Is this the way in which the ICRC is supposed to address the state committee? Is this the usual way to do it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go finish your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In obtaining the approval for the evacuation of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you answer the question, please, General, let's hear what -- it's all right. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document dove-tails with paragraphs 188 and 189 in my expert report regarding humanitarian aid where I explain how the humanitarian aid was set up and how those roots were set up and how all this functioned. At the state level there was the committee, and it was stipulated how it should go through the Main Staff, through the VRS, and all the way down to the actual implementation. And this indicates that it was addressed to the right body which was the state committee for the cooperation with international organisations, the coordination body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in your proofing session for this testimony, did you have an opportunity to see what General Nicolai said in his evidence on the 29th of November, 2008, at transcript page 18497 when he spoke about this evacuation and all the people who were involved in this evacuation? Because General Nicolai said here that it is not likely that General Gvero was actually at the meeting that this document is talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have an opportunity to look at the transcripts of General Nicolai's evidence. It was [indiscernible] translated to me. I had an opportunity to look at his interviews, his reports, and they formed a very good basis for the conclusions that I reached about all -- this issue, and I don't have anything to add to this statement made by General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kosovac. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Madam Fauveau, if you prefer to have the break now -- we should have a break in 17 minutes' time. But in other words you can start, and then we can have the break. Or else, if you prefer, we can have the break now and then you start and continue and finish. Whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I might as well start now and then have the break a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to submit to the witness Exhibit 5D7723. It is the note of General Milovanovic to General Miletic during the period of 31 December 1994. Could we please see page 2 in B/C/S. And if we could see the last paragraph please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this last paragraph, we see that it addresses the fact that General Miletic performed his duties and tasks in the framework of his functional position. If General Miletic during that period, namely in 1993, was at a given point in time the representative of the Chief of the Main Staff, should that fact have been written in this note, have appeared in this note?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer the question, please, General. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a question that my colleague had actually put to the witness on direct examination, and I don't see any need to readdress it on redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it did he derives from the last document that the Prosecutor submitted to the witness. I did not use this document, nor did I use the last document used by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we think the question is perfectly legitimate based on the use of these documents. So let's proceed with your answer, General, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I please be shown the previous page of this document? Very well. Your Honours, the part that I am now going to comment can also be seen in English. This is the lower part of the English text. It says here "the duties and situation in the service in the relevant period." This implies that whoever assesses an officer has to provide all the situations in the service that were observed during the relevant assessed period. It is well known, and I've said it already several times, that standing in for somebody is a situation in service. If at any -- if in any way General Miletic between 1990 and 1994, on the 31st of December, 1994, had stood in for the Chief of Staff in the staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, this should have been stated here. The period would have to be stated and the fact that he was standing in for him. In accordance with that, in the description on the next page, it has to be stated how the duty was performed. The assessment of an officer is precisely regulated by the rules of assessment. And skipping any of the things is checked by the personnel organs, and the assessment may be returned for review if they are not in compliance with this. My final answer would be this: This assessment on its first page and on the second page should show whether the -- the officer in question stood in for anybody during any period of time and whether that person was a Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you Exhibit P4133. And this is an UNPROFOR report dated the 29th of May until the 4th of June, 1995. I would need paragraph 14, page 5, please. I shall read out to you the sentence I am interested in which is in paragraph 14 which reads as follows: "[In English] However, with the current security situation and the lack of UNPROFOR escorts for convoys, UNHCR decided to suspend its convoys." [Interpretation] Does this sentence suggest in any way that the Republika Srpska authorities had refused the convoys to go through?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This sentence does not suggest any such thing in any of its parts. In a somewhat milder way, it represents the factual situation. Objectively, UNPROFOR had enough strength to accompany humanitarian aid, and this was never a problem. And also UNPROFOR was often late with notifying on the passage of humanitarian aid. And this is what you've asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit P4136. This is an UNPROFOR document. Could I have paragraph 2, please. This document is dated the 14th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, right at the beginning of the paragraph, we read that: "None of the UNHCR convoys to the enclaves have received clearances." These are the convoys that were going towards the enclaves. And we can see that the Srebrenica enclave convoy has been cancelled. As far as this document is concerned, I would like now to show you document 5D1429. This is a document that stems from the Main Staff. The document is dated the 12th of June, 1995. Since this document has not been translated, could you read out the first paragraph to us, i.e., the first three sentences.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We hereby inform you that we are in agreement with the approval issued by the coordination body for humanitarian aid of Republika Srpska, number 1351-HCR-816, which is relative to the implementation of the weekly plan of the UNHC Belgrade according to the following, and then Kotroman-Gorazde, Karakaj, Srebrenica," and thereafter it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The first date we can see was the 31st of June, but I think everybody will agree that this is not the 31st but the 13th of June. And then after that we can read the names of the enclaves. Without any translation, one can understand that on the 13th of June, in Gorazde, Karakaj, and Srebrenica, Sremska Raca, Bijeljina, Srebrenica. 14th of June, Karakaj, Srebrenica. 15th of June, Kotroman, Gorazde. Having seen this document, what can you say about the accuracy of this UN document; in other words, that not a single convoy was authorised to get through to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the document indicates that no convoy was approved or were late postponed, and this states the number of convoys and the quantity, this document excludes the accuracy of the previous document, i.e., the previous document is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would just ask if my colleague could show the witness the communication from the Main Staff to the UNPROFOR headquarters in Sarajevo with respect to the convoy, if she has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document is addressed to the Drina Corps and not to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that document. If the Prosecutor has this document, maybe he would like to give it to me during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't have it, I didn't pose the question, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's proceed, and then if we find it you can make good.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness document P4145. This is a press release on the UNHCR. I would like to see page 21, please. The bottom of the page, the chart we can see at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This table shows the humanitarian aid that reads Srebrenica in 1995. The shaded colour from -- well, July and -- June and July 1995. Save from the month of June, according to this diagram, what was the situation like in March, April, and May in 1995? Was there a drop in the humanitarian aid that reached the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this diagram, one can conclude that the humanitarian aid in eastern enclaves in May, April, May-February, and February are above the average of the quantities of humanitarian aid which were delivered, i.e., are very close to the peaks in the quantities of the humanitarian aid ever delivered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we possibly have our break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Madam. 25 minutes, thank you. Do you think you will finish -- or if you need us to have a shorter break, we will have a shorter break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be more prudent, but I will do my best and make sure that we can finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do I hear objections if we have 20 minutes instead of 25? No. Okay. Thank you. So break of 20 minutes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to show Exhibit P4203 to the witness now, please. This is a map which shows Sadjestvo operation, Exhibit 4203. Could we show the bottom right-hand corner of this map, please. Can we see the name of the person and the signature, which is not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We all know that Operation Sadjestvo was mentioned in Directive 7 and 7/1. Here we see the name of Manojlo Milovanovic and his signature below that. According to what you know about military matters, do you think Mr. Milovanovic could have drafted this map -- this map without any knowledge whatsoever of Directive 7 and 7/1?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please be shown the top of the map, its title? Yes. In practical terms, this map is the nucleolus of Directive 7/1. It arises from Directive 7, and this map could not be drafted by anybody who was not involved in the process from the beginning to end. Nobody could propose it for approval, because whoever signed it in the lower right-hand bottom had to explain to the commander the plan to the very last detail. It could be done by nobody else but that very person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document P45, which is an order stemming from the Main Staff dated 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My colleague suggested to you that it was on the 19th of January on page 3304. The document 03 was a document that was a document belonging to the Administration for Operations and Training. This document bears number 03, and I would like to show you the second page of this document now. On this document we see the name of General Milan Gvero. Why this -- why does this document not bear the name of General Miletic, General Mladic? It bears the number 03.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main and crucial thing about the -- where the document belongs is not where the document is filed. Where the document is filed means that it was entered in a protocol somewhere, and based on that, this is where the original copy will be kept, and from there it will be distributed. The belonging of a document can be seen from another number and the signatory who signed it. And these are the two elements that define a document. This document is not a document that originated from the Administration for Operations and Training. None of its elements point that it might be.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 1 of this document, please. Could the witness be shown item 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like you to look at items 1 and 2. Item 2 discusses a population and equipment, and item 3 discusses the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document P4209. I'm sorry, it's P4208. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, we maintain our position so far as providence of the document is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The position we took yesterday when it was put by Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall respond to that. This document was seised by the OTP on the premises of the Krajina 1st corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My learned friend will not respond like that. She will call evidence to that effect. She is not here to make statements and give evidence. She is here to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Let's proceed. He has just made his position clear, you can make yours as well, and then we will proceed. And then it's a question at the end of the day on what evidence we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall deal with this now. Could you look at item 2, please. In English this will be on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The last two lines speak about the treatment of prisoners and the civilian population, the handling of prisoners and the handling of the civilian population. I understand that you are not an expert in terms of psychological and moral support, but which body is in charge of the moral and psychological support?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was shown to me yesterday, and yesterday we had a lot of problems with it. By accident, the material stayed with me. I looked at the document yesterday evening. I offered the Prosecutor to return the document to them, and I made some very important notes about the document which is very important. The plan as such is an integral part and it has to exist, and every officer has to know that. The plan was signed, it seems, by the officers in charge of the sectors. As far as I can tell, this is Colonel Sokanovic, but I am not sure. The plan was approved by the commander, that's correct. I analysed that plan in detail, and I was able to see that no single element in the document can provide a guarantee that it belonged or was part of Sadjestvo 95.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, that was not my question. I would really like to be able to finish. I would like you to answer my question: Which body is in charge of moral and psychological support?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sector for moral --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you the penultimate page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Unsurprisingly, we would like the witness to finish when he was saying when he was interrupted by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Mr. Josse. Let's proceed, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the penultimate page of this document where we can see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It seems that my colleague has a few issues about the provenance and origin of this document. I would like to read out what Mr. Sokanovic said during his interview which took place on the 21st of October, 2004, regarding this particular document. On page 76 of this interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How is this admissible, Your Honour? How can the witness deal with this? Both points, as I've said, if my learned friend wants to try and get this through -- deal with the provenance, she needs to deal with it properly, not through the back door with this witness. The Court has already said that a statement made by a witness is not evidence. Put in this manner, I am not being very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave it. We don't want any lessons on how we should look at documents and their use during trial. I mean, we are perfectly capable about deciding later on about weight that we should give to each and every document that has been made use of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand. I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's proceed. Your question, have you finished it? Because I don't think you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet. 5D1428 on page 76. 76.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see in the middle of the page, this is in English, but the thing I am interested in is that the witness was -- or rather the representative of the OTP showed the witness 0886-8764, which is the ERN number of the document we seen a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the bottom of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Mr. Sokanovic what he said, the question was put too him: "Do you recognise who signed on behalf of General Gvero at the back?" [In English] "And Mr. Sokanovic responded by: "I can by chance. It's myself." [Interpretation] I believe you have already said this, but I am not quite sure. Does this make sense to you that Mr. Sokanovic actually signed the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you document 5D1417. Before this document is displayed, I would like to tell you that General Miletic was purportedly the third man of the Republika Srpska Army. This is a document dated the 19th of January, 30304. Since this document is not translated, could you read out the first paragraph which starts with the 5th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document. The date is 5th February.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: That is quite right. Could you please read out the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 5th of February, 1995, at Sarajevo airport a meeting was held of the joint central commission. The chair was the Chief of Staff of the UNPROFOR command, General Brickman. The delegation of RS was headed by Lieutenant-General Milan Gvero. The HVO delegation was headed by Major General Budimir, and the Muslim delegation by the brigade General Hadzihasanovic. The following decisions of the central joint commission were passed, adopted, and signed. The following decisions were passed, adopted, and signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before putting the question to you, I would like to show you 5D1418 which are those decisions taken by the central commission. Here we can see in the title that this is a meeting which was held on the 5th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the second page, please, the bottom of the second page. Here we can see the name "Gvero" right at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since this was chaired by the chief of the UNPROFOR, he was not a colonel. Why was it General Miletic? Do you have an explanation for this? Do you have an explanation for us why General Miletic at the time was a colonel. He was the third man in the Army of the Republika Srpska. Why did he not attend this meeting which was chaired by the Chief of Staff of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided my explanation very precisely. General Miletic could not be the third man in the Army Republika Srpska. If he had been, he would have certainly been there, but there is no option that would allow him to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D1419. This is a document which stems from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a report regarding the implementation of the cessation of hostilities on the 1st of January 1995. In this document, we see who attended this meeting, General Rose, who at the time was commanding UNPROFOR. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was represented here by General Alihahovic [phoen], and we had General Smith tell us that he was the second man in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was on the 7th of November, 2007, on transcript page number 1763. The Army of Republika Srpska was represented by General Tolimir and General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why, at the time General Miletic as a colonel did not attend this meeting? Do you have an explanation to give us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an explanation. My explanation was provided very precisely in the scheme entitled "Rank and Order." Neither by rank nor by order could General Miletic attend this meeting. Because before him by rank and by order, there was a huge number of generals and officers, and one can see that only assistant commanders were present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D1322. This is the agenda of Karadzic's secretary [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Diary, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have page 70 on the screen in B/C/S and page 59 in English. The 1st of June, 1995, entry which is precisely the period covered by the indictment. We can see here that a meeting was convened, attended by Mr. Krajisnik, Professor Koljevic, Prime Minister Kozic, Minister Buha Kalenic [phoen], the Minister Ninkovic, General Mladic, General Tolimir, and General Gvero were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us why General Miletic did not attend this kind of meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This type of meeting held at the highest level, when the president of state requires the presence of the highest state officials and the highest military officers, there is no place for General Miletic. He would not have any powers to act on anybody's behalf if he had been present at such a meeting. You can see that only the top echelons of the military were present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show you 5D1514. This is information stemming from the Main Staff dated the 31st of July, 1995. 5D1415.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I am interested in is this: Could we show the bottom of the document before turning to page 2. Page 2, could we show the bottom of page 2. This information has been put down on paper here by General Gvero. I would like to return now to page 1 of this document. At the end of the first paragraph, we can read as follows. I shall read it out to you in English: "[In English] The VRS Main Staff profoundly aware of the gravity and complexity of the situation has adopted the decision to undertake all measures by engaging the most senior officers of the Main Staff headed by the commander, General Mladic, and his assistant and transferring units from other sectors of the theater and in cooperation with the authorities to halt and smash the Ustasha aggression, liberate the temporarily occupied territory, and punish the aggressor." [Interpretation] Do you agree with -- do you agree with what General Gvero has written here; namely, that the commander and his assistants are the highest ranking officers in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. The sentence confirms the scheme that I drafted, the one about the rank and order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to get back to this. You have seen two orders today signed by General Miletic. One was dated August, and the other one was dated October. In light of this information whereby we see that the commander and his assistants left at the end of July, beginning of August to -- left for Eastern Bosnia. The fact that they signed the orders, do you think that this is quite normal? Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated this, and let me repeat, based on the fact that both orders required urgent response and that both orders relate to humanitarian aid, and humanitarian aid and assistance to the population, prove that General Miletic acted in accordance with the rules regarding the signing of those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, our client needed to be skewed excused, Your Honours. And he's specifically asked if the proceedings can stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think he will only be a minute, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I know, I know. I think we can wait. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us, does the fact that the commander and assistants of the commander were not present at the Main Staff, did that have any impact on the fact in a General Miletic signed certain documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This fact produces the obligation to sign documents that the most senior officer present has the right to sign, but it is very clearly specified what kind of documents we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My colleague read to you part of the statement of the witness Kesorovic in the Blagojevic case, and to be fair, vis-a-vis Mr. Kesorovic, I would like to correct some information that was submitted to you by my colleague. First of all, Mr. Kesorovic was in June 1995 a lieutenant-colonel, as declared on the 9th of June, 2004, page 10623 of the Blagojevic case. Then, he declared on page 10624: "[In English] I was in the military police department of the security administration of the sector for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The headquarters of my department was in Banja Luka in the building of the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps." [Interpretation] Does the fact that Lieutenant-Colonel Kesorovic was based in Banja Luka, could that have any impact on the way in which he perceived various members of the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka -- Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fact in relation to the previous time casts a different light. The first was based on the brief report, that was my view, that the fact that he didn't know meant that he didn't have to explain. But now, this fact may create an illusion on his part, because probably in communication with the basic command post, it was well known that General Miletic was there at most times and that created an illusion on his part that this was a man around whom everything revolved. And this assessment from Banja Luka, looking at the basic command post, may be very apparently a delusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to read out to you what General Skrbic, the assistant of the commander of the Main Staff for personnel administration stated before this Trial Chamber in this case on the 18th of September, 2007, on page 15596 in French. The Prosecutor asked the following question: "Were you at the same level of command as Miletic, or did you have the feeling, the impression that he was slightly above you or beneath you within the ministry?" I suppose he was referring to the Main Staff. And his answer, the answer of General Skrbic was the following: "He was beneath me in the hierarchy." Do you agree with this statement made by General Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, and figure 14 proves this. This shows clearly where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did General Skrbic who was the assistant of the commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army, would he have known the various levels of hierarchy within the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a similar post in the Army of Yugoslavia, and General Krstic ex officio was responsible, and he knew that. And I know, based on my personal knowledge, that he was very familiar with the chain of command and hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you say General Krstic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to repeat, General, because the interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I held a similar post in the Army of Yugoslavia, and the post that General Skrbic had in the Army of Republika Srpska, he was very much familiar with all that, and he was an expert in organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Perchance, the name of General Krstic was mentioned. We know that in July 1995 General Krstic was at the command -- forward command post in Zepa. When he was at that forward command post in Zepa, was he still the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the forward command post of the Drina Corps. I think that the first time when he went to the forward command post that he was not the corps commander. I didn't write down the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When he became commander of the corps, did the fact that he was at the forward command post, did that mean that he could no longer exercise the commander's duties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of any unit performs his duties from any location within its area, which means that he performed the duty when he was at the logistic forward -- logistic command post, when the unit was on the move, when he was at the forward command post, he was the commander. He performed the duties of a commander at all times.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did the situation of General Milovanovic who was at the forward command post in Western Bosnia any different from that of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not different in any aspect, and we can see that he performed the duty of the Chief of Staff successfully. He was the Chief of Staff at the forward command post, at the rear command post, while the unit -- units were on the move. Anywhere within the territory of Republika Srpska, he was the chief of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit P3312.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The report you already saw yesterday under P486, except for the fact that this version has been translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we call up page 18 in English and 19 in B/C/S, please. In B/C/S it's at the very bottom of the page. I would like to see paragraphs 88 and 89, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And I will read them out to you: "[In English] Violations of the Geneva Conventions were perpetrated by government sources when they refuse to allow the evacuation of the civilian population from Srebrenica, thus attempting to use them as a human shield. Civilians must be protected from what their own, as well as enemy forces regard as military expedient. "Serious allegations have been made against government forces regarding their offensive of December to January 1993. The facts can only be verified to an impartial investigation with the presence of international observers." [Interpretation] Do the events that are described in these two paragraphs have any relation with the number of people who were in Srebrenica during the spring of 1993, since we are dealing here with the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is linked with the number and with the actions at the time and actions taken after that time, and this is what I indicated at several places in my expert report and repeated here. This is something that I repeated once again when I indicated how causal relationships are to be studied and established.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D1427. It is a directive of the president of the republic dated the 6th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, did you know that the president of the republic issued other directives, directives that were not only military directives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I didn't read them, but he did have a basis to issue other directives.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show page 2 of this document to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since this document is not translated, would you please read out item 4 of this document to us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The presidents of the municipal assemblies and of the executive boards are obliged to comply with this directive immediately, and the governments of the republic is obliged to directly follow, direct, regularly inform about the implementation of the orders contained in this directive."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In light of this paragraph, did the president of the republic, his ministers and advisors, have the authority to consult the presidents of municipalities regarding the implementation of this directive?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole chain of information was set up in a special decree, and it was set up how information was to flow to and from the presidents of the municipal assemblies and the executive boards.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Document 6D324. I apologise, I am looking for the correct number. Perhaps 6D324. Is it 6D324?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We see here the directive of the president. Can you conclude on the basis of this document whether they were directives that were already adopted or were yet to be adopted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The directive was dated the 6th of August, 1994, and this is the -- 20-something August 1994, which means that this official note was based on the actions taking in accordance with the directive -- or, rather, the action was implementing the directive. And we can see that the contents here went a little bit beyond their competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. General, we've made it, at least. On behalf of my colleagues, I wish to thank you for having been patient with us, for having come over and stayed for such a long time to give and finish your testimony. And on behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you all success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse, now is your hour of the truth. What's the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is as follows. That we do not propose to call General Kovacevic, that I can confirm. I think it remains unlikely that we will wish to call any evidence. As a result of the re-examination that we have just heard from -- of this witness, we would like to contemplate whether we wish to add a witness to our list, but clearly that's not going to happen in the near future. And so I don't want to be in the least bit obstructive, but realistically, General Pandurevic's case is going to be able to start on Monday. There might be one thing we could do in the next six minutes, and that is hear the argument as to whether we are entitled to make an opening statement. And if we could have -- if it was possible to have a ruling on that in the next six minutes, then obviously that would -- well, that would help me personally. And I am happy to go first on this, and if I could just be given a moment, please. The Chamber will clearly need to look at Rule 84 which governs the making of opening statements. We have a number of arguments in the alternative. The first is that the rule envisages the possibility of the making of such a statement at the start of the case immediately after the Prosecution opening. At that juncture, whether the Defence will call any evidence is unknown, and it is of course possible that no evidence will be called; yet in those circumstances the accused through his Counsel will be entitled to an opening statement. And we ask why it is that an accused who chooses to postpone his right to an opening statement to the Defence stage of a case should be deprived of such a statement in those circumstances? Our second argument, perhaps more importantly, is as follows: We contend -- we have actually presented evidence. Firstly, we have presented a variety of exhibits through a large number of witnesses that the Chamber has heard over the last two-and-a-half years, and above all else we contend that we have presented a witness in the case of Djuro Djukic [phoen], through his 92 quater statement. We of course recognise that no decision has yet been made as to the admissibility of those statements, but nonetheless that is undoubtedly the presentation of evidence. Thirdly, my third alternative submission is really as follows: To stop us making an opening statement would not just be unfair, but particularly unfair bearing in mind we could have circumvented the problem by, for example, calling a character witness. That witness would have fulfilled any requirements that the rule might have. We've chosen not to do that because we take the view that would simply be wasting everyone's time, and we submit we shouldn't be deprived of making a statement because of that. And finally, and perhaps above all else, we really say that the Prosecution objection is rather petty. The Gvero Defence have, save the matters I've already alluded to, chosen to call little or no evidence. We are not going to trouble the Court in terms of much time. We are asking for no more than an hour, and I suspect it will take nearly three quarters of an hour to present some arguments at this stage in relation to our case. It isn't instead of a closing argument, it isn't instead of a final brief, but it's primarily to address why we've chosen to call no evidence. And in our submission, to deprive us of that opportunity at this particular juncture would be unfair, and as I've already said, rather petty, bearing in mind how little of the Court time we have actually consumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, very briefly, because Mr. Josse took almost five minutes of the six that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think he knows the reason you can start off with an opening statement is that you can change your mind and not -- decide not to put on any evidence. Defence Counsel -- Defence do that everyday. That's why the rule is that way. And I've seen it done many times, where you start -- you tell what your case is and you decide not to put on a case. You wait until the end, the only thing you can do is argue your case. He can't tell us anymore what his case is about. Now, on the other hand I am curious to hear what his case is and what he's going to say. If he could perhaps, in a minute, give us an outline of what he's going to say, but if he's going to get up and say why his client is not guilty, why they didn't put on a case, I mean, that's not what this is about. If he wants to take a minute and give us a brief preview of the coming attractions, I'm interested. I haven't objected to anything yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Have you -- yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a case which involves a number of accused. I don't know what my colleague wishes to talk about, but this could have an impact on the presentation of my case. The only thing I would like to draw your attention on is what Gvero's Defence lawyer has just said on line 3, page 25: "[In English] We contend we have actually presented evidence." [Interpretation] That is a matter to be addressed during our closing arguments. To allow my colleague to discuss evidence that has been shown and not entitle the other accused to do the same I believe would be extremely unfair for the other accused. It is not a formal objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a formal objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one last point, I am sure Counsel is aware that there are other rules here that allow statements to be made and that they can be afforded. So they are not completely shutdown from making a statement, or at least someone from that case making a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse and everyone else, for that matter, Mr. McCloskey as well. We did discuss this amongst ourselves, this morning, for example, and we are still undecided as to how to proceed. So we are not handing out our decision today, but what I suggest is, as an ex-Boy Scout, be prepared on Monday just in case we decide to authorise you to go ahead with your address, with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we will decide the issue first thing Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I certainly will be prepared. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a nice evening, and we will continue Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of January, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
